evidence: The brief and all three notes read as a small firm talking in first person (we/our/I) with business reasons attached to rules: instruction.md:1 'our clients keep emailing documents to whoever answered last'; conversations.md:31 'Our internet in court is patchy.'; conversations.md:9 'People fix typos and figures, so authors can edit their own messages.'; walls-and-retention.md:17 'because a leak is a professional-conduct problem for us'; integration.md:5 'we won't run an app that has them'; integration.md:7 'That means everything sent today has the same time, which is why we care that the order stays consistent.' Contractions appear throughout (doesn't, we'll, can't, mustn't, I'm, I've, won't, isn't, aren't). A grep for marketing/LLM gloss (seamless, robust, delve, leverage, ensure, comprehensive, intuitive, utilize, furthermore, moreover, additionally, em dashes) found zero hits across instruction.md and the notes. Requirements are written as varied-length prose, not numbered acceptance lists or perfectly parallel bullets; the only table is the account roster (walls-and-retention.md:5-11), which is data, not a spec matrix. The voice is consistent between instruction.md and the notes (same first-person firm voice, same plain register). Adversarial attempt: the notes are dense and requirement-heavy (e.g. walls-and-retention.md:17 enumerates every leak surface in one sentence; instruction.md:3 uses a 'First, ... Second, ...' structure, a mild LLM-ish pattern) and there are few true terse fragments, but each dense sentence is still tied to a firm-specific reason and phrased conversationally, so this does not reach 'robotic, over-polished, or LLM-generated prose'. Not a defect; at most a stylistic observation. This is a source-text judgement only; no runtime evidence is required for this row.
